title: JavaScript closures refresher
summary: You've written functions inside functions. Refresh what a closure keeps, and predict the classic loop and live-variable traps.
objective: Predict what closure code returns or logs, including shared loop variables and variables changed after the closure was made.

The loop only stops after `i++` makes `i` equal 3, so the shared `i` ends at 3, not 2.
The callbacks can still reach `i` after the loop ends; it hasn't gone anywhere.

bricks.title: A closure keeps the variable, not its value
bricks.body:
A closure is a function plus the variables in scope where it was made. Three rules predict almost everything:

1. It holds the **variable itself, not a copy**: later changes show up when it runs.
2. Each call of the outer function makes **fresh** variables, which outside code can reach only through the closure.
3. In a `for` loop, `let` makes a **new binding each iteration**; `var` makes **one**, shared by every closure.

bricks.prompt: Fill in what the last two calls return.

mistakes.feedback: `a` keeps its `count` between calls; it isn't reset to 0 each time.
Only `a` has been called so far, twice. Its `count` is 2.
`b` came from its own call to `makeCounter`, so it has its own `count`, starting at 0.
`b` doesn't share `a`'s `count`. Each call of `makeCounter` makes a fresh one.

bricks.explanation: `a` has called twice, so its `count` is 2. `b` has its own fresh `count`, so its first call returns 1.

options.feedback: That assumes the closure copied `name` when it was made. It holds the variable, which now says Grace.
`name` is in scope when `greet` runs and holds a string, so nothing is undefined.
`name` is declared with `let`, so reassigning it is fine. Only `const` would throw.

bricks.explanation: `greet` reads `name` when it's called, not when it was created. By then `name` holds `'Grace'`.

bricks.prompt: What does the last line log?

options.feedback: `w.balance` is a new property on the returned object. The `balance` that `deposit` closes over is a separate variable, still 0.
`balance` starts at 0 and `10` is a number, so `0 + 10` is a plain number.

options.text: A `TypeError`: you can't set properties on the wallet
options.feedback: The returned object is ordinary, so adding `w.balance` works. It just doesn't touch the closed-over variable.

bricks.hint: Is `w.balance` the same thing as the `balance` inside `createWallet`?
bricks.explanation: Outside code can reach `balance` only through `deposit`. Setting `w.balance` adds an unrelated property, so `deposit(10)` adds to 0 and returns 10.

bricks.prompt: Every button logs `Clicked button 3`. Tap the line that causes it.
bricks.hint: Which line decides whether each handler gets its own `i`?
bricks.explanation: `var i` on line 2 makes one `i` shared by all handlers, and it's 3 by the time anyone clicks. Changing it to `let` gives each handler its own `i`.

challenge.prompt: What does the last line log?

options.feedback: You got `i` right, but `label` is one variable that every closure holds. It says `'row'` by the time they run.
You got `label` right, but this loop uses `let`, so each closure has its own `i`: 0, 1 and 2.
Both mixed up: `let` gives each closure its own `i`, and `label` was changed to `'row'` before they ran.

challenge.hint: Check each variable separately: how many copies of it exist, and what it holds when the functions run?
challenge.explanation: Each closure has its own `i` (0, 1, 2) from `let`, but all share the one `label`, which is `'row'` when `map` calls them.

takeaways: A closure reads its variables when it runs, so expect their latest values, not the ones at creation.
Each call of the outer function makes fresh variables, private to the closures it returns.
Closures in a loop: use `let` for one variable per iteration; `var` gives every closure the same one.
